title: VeriPol flags 25 and 39 false robbery reports in Murcia and Málaga in a one-week 2017 pilot; Spain's police drop it in 2024
summary: The Spanish National Police's VeriPol text classifier flagged 25 false robbery reports in Murcia and 39 in Málaga in a June 2017 pilot week; the police stopped using it on 21 October 2024.
account: VeriPol, a model for detecting false robbery reports from their text, was developed by researchers at the Complutense and Carlos III universities with police officer Miguel Camacho-Collados. A pilot study in Murcia and Málaga ran for one week in June 2017. The model appeared in Knowledge-Based Systems (Quijano-Sánchez, Liberatore, Camacho-Collados and Camacho-Collados, 2018). The abstract reports a validation accuracy of 91% on more than 1,000 reports from 2015, an improvement of more than 15% over expert officers. It reports that the pilot study showed a lower bound on empirical precision of about 83%. Civio reported that the Interior Ministry announced nationwide use in 2018. Scientific American (1 February 2019) reported that the one-week pilot in Murcia and Málaga detected 25 and 39 false robberies respectively, against 3 and 12 in the same month over the previous decade. It quoted Camacho Collados on colleagues wasting time on cases that never occurred. According to Civio, the police analyzed 49,702 complaints in 2019 and deemed 2,338 of them false. AlgorithmWatch (27 October 2020) found no independent verification of effectiveness since deployment. Civio reported that in 2022 the police analyzed 3,762 complaints and deemed 511 of them false. In a University of Valencia report of September 2024, Lucía Martínez Garay and colleagues criticized the training sample of 1,122 reports, the missing officer training and the missing regional language variation. They found that the 2017 pilot paper gave neither case counts nor a confusion matrix. The police told them that VeriPol still needed an evaluation of its performance that had not been possible to carry out. The Interior Ministry told Civio that the police stopped using VeriPol on 21 October 2024. Civio (25 March 2025) reported that the Ministry said that the police stopped because the tool was not valid in judicial proceedings. Civio also reported that the police said that in 83.54% of reports flagged false the complainant confessed.
purpose: Estimate the probability that a robbery report is false from its text to support police decisions.

The developers ran the pilot themselves, and independent researchers note that the paper gives no case counts or confusion matrix.

fields.summary: The Spanish National Police's VeriPol text classifier flagged 25 false robbery reports in Murcia and 39 in Málaga in a June 2017 pilot week; the police stopped using it on 21 October 2024.
fields.account: VeriPol, a model for detecting false robbery reports from their text, was developed by researchers at the Complutense and Carlos III universities with police officer Miguel Camacho-Collados. A pilot study in Murcia and Málaga ran for one week in June 2017. The model appeared in Knowledge-Based Systems (Quijano-Sánchez, Liberatore, Camacho-Collados and Camacho-Collados, 2018). The abstract reports a validation accuracy of 91% on more than 1,000 reports from 2015, an improvement of more than 15% over expert officers. It reports that the pilot study showed a lower bound on empirical precision of about 83%. Civio reported that the Interior Ministry announced nationwide use in 2018. Scientific American (1 February 2019) reported that the one-week pilot in Murcia and Málaga detected 25 and 39 false robberies respectively, against 3 and 12 in the same month over the previous decade. It quoted Camacho Collados on colleagues wasting time on cases that never occurred. According to Civio, the police analyzed 49,702 complaints in 2019 and deemed 2,338 of them false. AlgorithmWatch (27 October 2020) found no independent verification of effectiveness since deployment. Civio reported that in 2022 the police analyzed 3,762 complaints and deemed 511 of them false. In a University of Valencia report of September 2024, Lucía Martínez Garay and colleagues criticized the training sample of 1,122 reports, the missing officer training and the missing regional language variation. They found that the 2017 pilot paper gave neither case counts nor a confusion matrix. The police told them that VeriPol still needed an evaluation of its performance that had not been possible to carry out. The Interior Ministry told Civio that the police stopped using VeriPol on 21 October 2024. Civio (25 March 2025) reported that the Ministry said that the police stopped because the tool was not valid in judicial proceedings. Civio also reported that the police said that in 83.54% of reports flagged false the complainant confessed.
